lessons.title: Implicit Binding Rules in Object Methods
lessons.description: When a function is called as an object method, 'this' refers to that object.

sections.heading: What is 'this'?
paragraphs: this is a special keyword that refers to the object the function is called on. Its value depends on how the function is called — not where it's defined. This is called dynamic binding.
list: In a method call (obj.method()), this = the object (obj)
In a plain function call, this = global object (or undefined in strict mode)
In a constructor, this = the newly created object
Arrow functions don't have their own this — they inherit from the parent

codeExamples.heading: Implicit binding with object methods
explanation: When the function is detached and called alone, this loses the binding.
This is the most common this bug — losing implicit binding.
Arrow functions fix this by inheriting this from the enclosing scope.

practice.task: Create an object with a name property and a method that logs this.name. Call the method directly, then assign it to a variable and call it. Observe the difference.
hints: Detached call: let fn = obj.method; fn() — this = undefined (strict) or global.

keyTakeaways: this depends on how a function is called, not where it's defined.
Implicit binding: when called as a method, this = the object.
Losing binding is common — the function is called without its object context.
Arrow functions solve this by inheriting this from the enclosing scope.
lessons.challenge: Write code that demonstrates implicit binding, lost binding, and the arrow function fix side by side.

lessons.title: Explicit Binding: call(), apply(), and bind()
lessons.description: Force a specific 'this' value using call, apply or bind.

sections.heading: Three ways to set 'this' explicitly
list: func.call(thisArg, arg1, arg2) — calls immediately with a specific this
func.apply(thisArg, [args]) — same but args as an array
func.bind(thisArg) — returns a new function with 'this' permanently set
All three accept any object as the first argument (including null/undefined)

codeExamples.heading: call, apply, and bind
explanation: apply is identical to call but takes arguments as an array.
bind doesn't call the function — it returns a new one with this locked in.
bind is most useful for callbacks where you need a consistent this.

practice.task: Write a function that logs this.value. Use call, apply and bind to call it with 3 different objects, each with a different value property.
hints: Use func.bind(obj) to create a permanently bound function.

keyTakeaways: call() and apply() invoke the function immediately with a custom this.
bind() returns a new function with this permanently set — it doesn't invoke.
Use bind() when passing callbacks that need a specific this.
These methods let you borrow functions from one object and use them with another.
lessons.challenge: Use bind to create a debounce function that delays calling a function until after a specified wait time.

lessons.title: Constructor Function Binding with the new Operator
lessons.description: When using 'new', JavaScript creates a fresh object and sets 'this' to it.

sections.heading: How 'new' works
paragraphs: When you call a function with new, JavaScript does four things: creates a new empty object, sets this to that object, links the prototype, and returns the object.
list: Sets this inside the function to the new object
Links the object's prototype to the function's prototype
Returns the object (unless the function explicitly returns another object)

codeExamples.heading: Constructor function pattern
explanation: new User("Alex", 25) creates a fresh object and sets this to it.
Each new call creates an independent object.
instanceof confirms the object was created by that constructor.
This is the pre-ES6 way to create objects — classes are syntactic sugar over this pattern.

practice.task: Create a constructor function Book(title, author) that stores the title and author on this. Create 2 book instances and log their properties.
hints: Define function Book(title, author) { this.title = title; this.author = author; }.

keyTakeaways: new creates a fresh object and sets this to it.
Constructor functions define blueprints for creating multiple similar objects.
Each new call produces an independent instance.
ES6 classes are syntactic sugar over constructor functions and prototypes.
lessons.challenge: Rewrite the User constructor function as an ES6 class. Verify the behavior is identical.

lessons.title: Lexical this Binding in Arrow Functions
lessons.description: Arrow functions don't have their own 'this' — they inherit it from the surrounding scope.

sections.heading: Arrow functions and 'this'
paragraphs: Arrow functions were designed to solve the this problem. They don't create their own this — instead, they use the this of the enclosing scope (lexical this).
list: Arrow functions inherit this from the parent scope
They don't have their own this, even when used as methods
call, apply and bind don't affect arrow function this
Perfect for callbacks inside methods — this always refers to the object

codeExamples.heading: Arrow function fixes this binding
explanation: The regular function callback creates its own this — it's the global object, not user.
The arrow function doesn't create its own this — it inherits this from showHobbiesNew.
This is the primary use case for arrow functions — callbacks that need the outer this.
Don't use arrow functions as object methods — they lose implicit binding.

practice.task: Create an object with a timer method that logs this.name every second. First use a regular function in setInterval (broken), then fix it with an arrow function.
hints: Arrow functions inherit this from the enclosing method.

keyTakeaways: Arrow functions don't have their own this — they inherit from the enclosing scope.
This makes them perfect for callbacks that need the outer this.
Don't use arrow functions as object methods — they break implicit binding.
call, apply, and bind have no effect on arrow function this.
lessons.challenge: Refactor a class-like object that uses forEach callbacks. Replace all regular function callbacks with arrow functions and explain each change.
